overview: Qataban was an ancient South Arabian kingdom centred on Wadi Bayhan in today’s Yemen. Its capital Timna linked irrigated farming communities with incense caravans. The imported map covers 323 to 1 BCE, only part of a history extending into the early centuries CE. Its broad southern-Yemen outline includes places outside the kingdom’s documented heartland and should not be read as a surveyed frontier. Saba and Hadramawt were neighbouring kingdoms with their own histories.

periods.title: The mapped caravan kingdom
periods.summary: The map shows four snapshots of Qataban’s region; these boundaries and endpoints do not establish its complete historical lifetime.

sections.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water

items.text: Timna’s location on Wadi Bayhan helped connect Indian Ocean commerce with routes towards the Mediterranean. The excavation project places Qataban among southern Arabia’s leading powers from the sixth to first centuries BCE. Incense traffic relied on a substantial urban and agricultural hinterland.

A granite pillar in Timna’s market carries royal commercial regulations on all four sides. Nearby excavations uncovered ten houses. Government could make its rules physically present where merchants worked: a stone noticeboard was much harder to misplace than a loose sheet.

The stone-paved Najd Marqad road linked the commercial corridor between Timna and Haribat. Yemen’s heritage submission describes this surviving mountain route alongside settlements, fields and caravan facilities. Trade required a connected landscape, including the difficult ground between cities.

Farmers diverted seasonal floodwater into fields through branching channels. Water usually involved local management, but stronger kings also regulated distribution and commissioned major works. Controlling the flow could determine which downstream fields received a drink after the rain.

A fifth-century BCE decree discussed by Charbonnier ordered an upstream area kept clear of obstructions so floodwater could reach land below. This predates the map’s first snapshot. Another inscription records a father and son digging a well in their palm grove: water infrastructure could also be a family undertaking.

sections.title: At home: meals, names and games

items.text: Plant remains at Hajar Ibn Humayd include barley, millet, cumin, sesame, flax and grapevine, according to Charbonnier’s archaeological synthesis. These are clues to the valley’s crops across its ancient occupation, rather than the contents of one dated dinner. The menu was much more varied than incense!

Some Timna houses advertised their names in façade inscriptions, including bayt Yaʿūd. Stone bases supported upper construction of mudbrick and timber lattice. Charred uprights date some building work to the late fourth or early third century BCE. A house name could survive long after its roof collapsed.

House Yafash yielded containers, a burned comb and a stone die. These small objects bring grooming, storage and gaming into a picture often dominated by temples and kings. The house’s destruction belongs to the first century CE in the Smithsonian account, after this map record ends.

Two bronze lions from House Yafash each carry a small boy on their backs. The museum dates them to about 75 BCE to 50 CE. Artists cast the lions and riders separately using the lost-wax technique. These were extraordinary decorations; actual children were not being issued lion transport.

The bronze bases name Thuwayb and Aqrab of the Muhasni family as the people who decorated Yafash. Archaeologists therefore have both objects from a home and words identifying its patrons. The names help turn an anonymous ruin into a place where particular people made choices.

sections.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name

items.text: In Timna’s northwestern sector, inscriptions identify a courtyard sanctuary of Athirat. Founded around the fourth or third century BCE, it was repeatedly altered. Its rear wall also formed part of the city perimeter: religious buildings and the settlement’s boundary could share the same masonry.

Another monumental building, TT1, was first called an Athtar temple because of one inscription. The Metropolitan Museum’s later catalogue considers a palace more likely. Revising a building’s label can change our picture of royal and religious space without moving a single stone.

At Hayd ibn Aqil, large family tombs had central corridors and long chambers with shelves for the dead. Some funerary stelae survived in place despite ancient looting elsewhere. Relatives were remembered together in deliberately arranged spaces, giving archaeologists evidence about commemoration as well as carving.

A third-century BCE alabaster figure now in Toledo Museum of Art is about 47 centimetres tall and has inlaid shell eyes. Its likely origin is the cemetery near Timna, but that findspot is not securely documented. The luminous stone and carefully treated eyes made a striking memorial.

The same statue’s base carries a South Arabian inscription transcribed by the museum as “ʾbydʿ ḏ-Ḏmrʾl”, translated “Abī-yadaʿ son of Damar’ali”. This is a scholarly Latin-letter rendering of the ancient writing, not modern Arabic or the original letter shapes. It preserves a person’s name and lineage from the third century BCE.

ending.text: Qataban did not fall at the map’s 1 BCE cutoff. Hadramawt eventually annexed the kingdom. Published summaries differ between the first and second centuries CE, so a single exact year would mislead. Timna’s destruction and the political annexation are separate questions. The loss of Qataban’s kingship was not the disappearance of southern Arabia’s farming communities or commercial traditions.
